rw: Shareholders risk only the money they invested, and creditors cannot go after their personal assets, which makes limited liability a defining feature of the corporate form.

ww.No separate legal identity at all: A corporation is a distinct legal person, separate from its owners, so the claim of no separate legal identity at all is the opposite of the truth.
ww.Unlimited personal liability for owners: Unlimited personal liability describes sole proprietors and general partners, whose own assets can be reached for business debts, while corporation owners are shielded from that exposure.
ww.A single owner who is the business: A single owner who is the business describes a sole proprietorship, since a corporation is a legal entity separate from the people who own its shares.

rw: Two or more partners pool their skills, knowledge and money, which a one person sole proprietorship cannot do, so this is a real advantage of the partnership form.

ww.Profits are never shared with any partne: Partners normally share profits according to their agreement, so saying profits are never shared with any partner contradicts how a partnership is set up and run.
ww.There is only one decision maker in the: Having only one decision maker is a trait of a sole proprietorship, so it cannot be an advantage that a partnership has over it.
ww.Partners avoid all personal liability fo: General partners usually remain personally liable for the firm's debts, so avoiding all personal liability is false and is more typical of a corporation or limited partner.

rw: A C corporation pays corporate income tax on its profits and shareholders pay tax again on dividends received, which is the classic double taxation of this structure.

ww.An LLC firm: An LLC is generally a pass through entity, so its profits are taxed once on the owners' personal returns, not twice at the business and owner levels.
ww.Sole proprietor: A sole proprietor reports business income directly on a personal return, so it is taxed just once and there is no separate business tax level to double up.
ww.Partnership: Partnership income passes through to the partners, who pay tax on their shares personally, so the firm itself pays no income tax and no double taxation arises.

rw: Banking and insurance sell intangible help and expertise rather than physical goods, which is exactly what defines a service business such as a bank or insurer.

ww.A farming business: Farming grows crops or raises animals, which means it produces goods and belongs to the primary sector, not the businesses that provide banking or insurance services.
ww.A mining business: Mining extracts raw materials such as coal or metals from the ground, so it produces a tangible resource and does not provide an intangible service like insurance.
ww.A retail business: A retail business sells finished goods to consumers, which is selling products, while banking and insurance are intangible services and fit a different category.

rw: A nonprofit may earn revenue, but any surplus is reinvested in its mission and not distributed to owners, which is the key difference from a for profit firm.

ww.It is not permitted to earn any revenue: Nonprofits are allowed to earn revenue from programs, fees and services, and many do, so a ban on earning any revenue is false and not the real difference.
ww.It pays no wages or salaries to any of i: Nonprofits can pay reasonable wages and salaries to staff and managers, so claiming they pay none to anyone is untrue and misses the real difference, which is profit distribution.
ww.It is owned by shareholders who receive: Shareholders who collect the profits describe a for profit corporation, while a nonprofit has no owners who receive profit, so this option describes the opposite organization.

rw: In a market economy, the interaction of what buyers want and what sellers offer moves prices up or down until the market clears, so supply and demand set prices.

ww.The state government: A state government setting prices is characteristic of a command economy, while in a market economy buyers and sellers interacting set prices without central direction.
ww.A worker committee: A worker committee setting prices is not how market economies work, since prices come from the decisions of many buyers and sellers and not from any single body.
ww.Tradition and custom: Tradition and custom guide decisions in a traditional economy, where habits are handed down, but a market economy relies on prices that respond to supply and demand.

rw: In a command economy, a central authority, usually the government, decides what goods to make, how much, and for whom, so planners hold the main decisions.

ww.Village elders by custom: Village elders deciding by custom describes a traditional economy, where inherited practices guide production, whereas a command economy uses formal central plans.
ww.Competing private firms: Competing private firms making production choices is the mark of a market economy, while in a command economy the state limits private firms and sets output.
ww.Individual consumers: Individual consumers steering production through their purchases is characteristic of a market economy, not a command economy where central planners override consumer demand.

rw: The United States is mainly market driven but the government also regulates, taxes, and provides services such as roads and Social Security, which makes it a mixed economy.

ww.A command economy: The United States is not run by central planners who dictate output, and private firms make most decisions, so labeling it a command economy is wrong.
ww.A tradition economy: A tradition economy relies on custom and inherited methods, which does not describe the modern, technology driven United States where markets and laws guide most choices.
ww.A market economy: Calling it purely a market economy ignores the large government role in regulation, taxation and public programs, so the more accurate label is a mixed economy.

rw: Capitalism rests on individuals and firms owning businesses and resources and seeking profit, so private ownership is the typical characteristic of this system.

ww.Production based on tradition and custom: Production based on tradition and custom defines a traditional economy, whereas capitalism relies on private owners and market incentives rather than inherited habits.
ww.Fixed prices set by the central planners: Fixed prices set by central planners belong to a command economy, while capitalism lets prices move freely with supply and demand instead of being decided by planners.
ww.State ownership of all the major industr: State ownership of all major industries is a feature of socialism or communism, and it is the reverse of capitalism, in which individuals and firms own businesses.

rw: Every society has limited resources, so each must decide what goods to make, how to make them, and who receives them, and these three questions apply to any system.

ww.Where to advertise, when and how often t: Advertising decisions are business choices within a firm and are not basic questions that every economic system must settle about producing and distributing goods.
ww.Which currency to use and which bank to: Choosing a currency or bank is a financial detail, not one of the basic allocation questions about production and distribution that all economic systems face.
ww.Who to tax, when to tax and why to do so: Taxation is a government policy matter, not one of the three core questions of what, how and for whom that every economy must answer.

rw: In a traditional economy, people do what their ancestors did, so decisions about producing and sharing goods follow custom and past practice from one generation to the next.

ww.Government plans and rules: Government plans and rules guide a command economy, whereas a traditional economy leans on long standing customs rather than on formal directives from authorities.
ww.International agreements: International agreements shape trade between countries but do not form the basis of a traditional economy, where local customs and inherited roles guide decisions.
ww.Market prices and profits: Market prices and profits drive decisions in a market economy, while a traditional economy follows established practice instead of responding to price signals.

rw: Fiscal policy is the use of government taxation and spending to influence the economy, such as cutting taxes or increasing spending to boost demand.

ww.Labor policy: Labor policy covers employment rules such as wages and working conditions, and it does not work mainly through government taxing and spending to steer the economy.
ww.Trade policy: Trade policy deals with tariffs, quotas and agreements on imports and exports, rather than with using taxes and government spending to influence overall economic activity.
ww.Monetary policy: Monetary policy is run by the central bank through interest rates and the money supply, not through government taxing and spending, so it does not fit this definition.

rw: The Fed carries out monetary policy by influencing interest rates and the money supply, for example through its policy rate and open market operations, to guide growth and inflation.

ww.Setting the tax rates that all businesse: Setting business tax rates is done by Congress and tax authorities under fiscal policy, not by the Federal Reserve, whose monetary tools work through interest rates.
ww.Passing the laws that businesses must fo: Passing laws is the job of Congress, a legislative body, whereas the Federal Reserve is a central bank that manages money and credit conditions.
ww.Setting the prices that stores charge fo: The Federal Reserve does not set store prices, since prices in the economy are determined by markets, and the Fed works through interest rates and the money supply.

rw: Antitrust laws break up or block monopolies and anticompetitive practices like price fixing, which protects competition and gives consumers lower prices and more choice.

ww.To set the minimum wage for all workers: Minimum wage rules come from labor law, not antitrust law, which targets anticompetitive behavior by firms rather than the pay floor for workers.
ww.To tax imports at the border of each cou: Taxing imports is a trade policy done through tariffs and has nothing to do with antitrust laws, which deal with competition among domestic and other firms.
ww.To guarantee steady profits for large fi: Antitrust laws do the reverse of guaranteeing profits, since they keep large firms from dominating markets and leave their success to competition.

rw: Lower taxes leave households more to spend and higher government spending adds demand directly, so the aim is to stimulate demand and economic activity during the downturn.

ww.Reduce the national debt and the deficit: Cutting taxes and raising spending increases the deficit and adds to debt, so reducing the national debt is not the goal; the government accepts a bigger deficit.
ww.Raise interest rates to cool the economy: Raising interest rates is a tightening monetary action that cools demand, while the government in this case is using fiscal stimulus to push demand up, not down.
ww.Slow down inflation across the whole nat: Slowing inflation requires reducing demand, but cutting taxes and raising spending adds demand, so the policy fits a recession and not an effort to cool prices.

rw: A subsidy is financial support from the government to a business or industry, such as a farm payment, which lowers costs or raises income for producers.

ww.A tax placed on goods that are brought i: A tax on goods brought in from other lands is a tariff, not a subsidy, because a subsidy is money that the government gives rather than collects.
ww.A limit on the amount of a product that: A limit on how much of a product may be produced is a quota or production cap, which restricts supply, while a subsidy supports producers with money.
ww.A fine charged to a company for breaking: A fine charged for breaking a regulation is a penalty paid to the government, the opposite of a subsidy, which is a payment from the government.

rw: At a capped price below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, so more people want the good than producers will sell, which is a shortage.

ww.A surplus: A ceiling below equilibrium makes the price too low, so buyers want more than sellers supply, which creates a shortage rather than a surplus of goods.
ww.A higher price: A ceiling is a legal maximum, so it cannot push the price above equilibrium; when set below it, the controlled price is lower, not higher.
ww.No change: A binding price ceiling changes the market outcome by holding the price under equilibrium, so there is a gap between demand and supply and not no change.

rw: Profit is what remains from sales after all costs are paid, so it equals total revenue minus total cost, positive when revenue is higher and negative otherwise.

ww.Price times the quantity sold: Price times quantity sold gives total revenue, which ignores what it cost to produce the goods, so it is not profit.
ww.Total revenue plus total cost: Adding revenue and cost together has no economic meaning for profit, since costs reduce what a firm keeps rather than adding to it.
ww.Total cost minus total revenue: Subtracting revenue from cost reverses the formula, and it would show a negative number whenever the firm actually earns a profit, so it is not the right calculation.

rw: Flour and sugar are inputs used up as more goods are made, so the amount spent rises and falls with output, which makes them variable costs.

ww.The owner's salary: An owner's salary is fixed regardless of how many loaves are baked, so it is a fixed cost and does not change with the level of output.
ww.Insurance premium: An insurance premium is typically a set periodic amount that does not rise or fall with how much the bakery produces, so it is a fixed cost.
ww.Monthly rent: Monthly rent stays the same whether the bakery bakes a few loaves or thousands, which makes it a fixed cost and not a variable one.

rw: Each unit contributes 20 minus 8, or 12 dollars, toward fixed costs, so break even is 6,000 divided by 12, which equals 500 units.

ww.214 units: The figure 214 comes from dividing 6,000 by 28, adding the unit cost to the price, but break even uses the margin of 20 minus 8, which is 12.
ww.750 units: The number 750 comes from dividing 6,000 by the unit cost of 8, but the right divisor is the 12 dollar margin per unit, so it overshoots.
ww.300 units: The number 300 comes from dividing 6,000 by the price of 20, ignoring that each unit costs 8 to make; the margin of 12 gives 500 units.

rw: Marginal cost is the additional cost incurred to produce one more unit of output, which helps firms decide whether expanding production adds more cost than revenue.

ww.The average cost of all the units: The average cost of all units is average total cost, found by dividing total cost by quantity, which differs from the cost of just one extra unit.
ww.The cost of the first unit only: The cost of the first unit alone is not marginal cost in general, because marginal cost is measured for whichever additional unit is being considered at the time.
ww.The total of all the fixed costs: Total fixed costs are expenses that do not change with output, whereas marginal cost concerns the extra cost of one more unit, which is usually a variable cost.

rw: An annual insurance premium on a factory is charged at the same amount however many goods are produced, so it is a fixed cost for the business.

ww.Raw materials used in making each produc: Raw materials are consumed in each product, so the total spent grows with output, which makes them a variable cost and not a fixed cost.
ww.Sales commissions paid to sellers on eac: Sales commissions rise as more sales are made, so the total paid changes with output, which makes this a variable cost rather than a fixed one.
ww.Packaging supplies used to wrap each uni: Packaging supplies are used up with each unit sold, so total spending grows with output, which means they are variable costs and not fixed costs.

rw: Economies of scale occur when increasing output spreads fixed costs over more units and improves efficiency, so the average cost per unit falls as production rises.

ww.When the total cost rises faster than th: When total cost rises faster than output, the cost per unit increases, which signals diseconomies of scale, the opposite of economies of scale.
ww.When a business produces fewer and fewer: Producing fewer units does not lower the average cost; economies of scale involve expanding output so that the cost per unit falls, not shrinking production.
ww.When prices are set by the government fo: Government set prices are unrelated to scale economies, which arise inside a firm as it grows, spreading fixed costs and gaining efficiency, not from price controls.

rw: GDP is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period, usually a quarter or year.

ww.The average price of a standard basket o: The average price of a basket of goods bought by households is measured by the Consumer Price Index, not GDP, which measures production.
ww.The number of people who have jobs in th: The count of employed people relates to employment statistics, whereas GDP measures the value of output produced and not how many individuals have jobs.
ww.The total spending of the government ove: Government spending is only one component of GDP, so total government outlays cannot be what GDP measures, since GDP covers all final output in the economy.

rw: The unemployment rate is the number of unemployed job seekers divided by the labor force, expressed as a percent, so it counts only people actively seeking work.

ww.All adults without jobs as a share of pe: Counting all adults without jobs would include retirees, students and others not looking for work, which overstates unemployment, since the labor force is the proper base.
ww.The number of job openings divided by ap: Job openings divided by applicants is a measure of labor market tightness and not the unemployment rate, which is based on the labor force.
ww.The number of people who quit last year: The number of people who quit last year is a measure of job turnover, and it does not give the share of the labor force that is unemployed.

rw: Inflation is a general, sustained rise in the level of prices across the economy, which reduces what each unit of money can buy over time.

ww.An increase in unemployment levels: A rise in unemployment is a labor market change, not inflation, which is defined by rising prices rather than the number of people without jobs.
ww.A fall in the price of one product: A fall in the price of a single product is a relative price change, not inflation, which refers to a broad rise in prices generally.
ww.A rise in the value of the dollar: A rise in the dollar's value would make money worth more, which is nearly the opposite of what inflation does, since inflation erodes purchasing power.

rw: The CPI tracks how the prices of a typical basket of goods and services bought by households change over time, making it a common inflation measure.

ww.The total value of the goods a country s: The total value of goods a country sells abroad is its exports, a trade figure, and not the CPI, which tracks consumer prices.
ww.The interest rate that lenders charge on: The interest rate lenders charge is the cost of borrowing and is not what the CPI measures, since the CPI follows consumer prices.
ww.The number of businesses operating in on: The number of businesses in an area is a count of firms and has nothing to do with the CPI, which is a price index.

rw: A recession is a significant decline in economic activity spread across the economy and lasting several months, usually seen in falling output, employment and income.

ww.A one-day fall in the value of the stock: A one day stock market fall is a short market move and does not meet the definition of a recession, which involves broad weakness lasting months.
ww.A period of rapid price rises across the: Rapid price rises across the economy describe inflation, not a recession, which is defined by a decline in output and activity rather than in prices.
ww.A rise in the amount that the government: A rise in government spending is a fiscal action, often used to fight a recession, and it does not define one.

rw: Imports are goods and services that a country buys from producers in other countries, bringing foreign made products to domestic buyers.

ww.Goods produced and sold at home to local: Goods produced and sold at home are domestic goods and do not cross a border, so they cannot be imports, which come from other countries.
ww.Goods sold to other countries by local f: Goods sold to other countries by local firms are exports, not imports, since imports flow into the country from foreign producers.
ww.Taxes on foreign goods that enter the co: Taxes on foreign goods that enter the country are tariffs, and a tariff is a charge on imports, not the imported goods themselves.

rw: Comparative advantage means a country should specialize in goods whose opportunity cost is lower than other countries', because giving up less output creates gains from trade.

ww.A higher opportunity cost: Producing goods at a higher opportunity cost would mean giving up more of other output, which is the opposite of what comparative advantage recommends.
ww.The same cost as the others: Making goods at the same cost as others gives no comparative advantage and no gains from trade, since specialization pays only when costs differ.
ww.The highest possible price: The highest possible price is not the test; comparative advantage is about relative opportunity cost of production, not the price at which goods are sold.

rw: A trade deficit means the value of imports is greater than the value of exports, so the country buys more from abroad than it sells.

ww.Its exports exceed its imports: When exports exceed imports a country has a trade surplus, not a deficit, because it sells more abroad than it buys from other countries.
ww.It has no trade with others: A country with no trade has balanced trade at zero and neither a surplus nor a deficit, so the situation is not a trade deficit.
ww.Its state spends more than it gets: A government spending more than it receives has a budget deficit, which is different from a trade deficit, since that one concerns imports and exports.

rw: A stronger dollar means each euro buys fewer dollars, so U.S. goods cost more in euros and European buyers tend to purchase fewer of them.

ww.They become cheaper for European buyers: A stronger dollar raises the price of U.S. goods in euros, so exports become more expensive for European buyers and not cheaper.
ww.They are banned automatically by the gov: Exchange rate moves are market outcomes and are not banned by governments, so exports are not automatically prohibited when the dollar strengthens against the euro.
ww.They are unaffected by the change in the: When the dollar strengthens, a European buyer needs more euros to buy the same dollar priced good, so export demand is affected and not unaffected.

rw: A free trade agreement lowers or removes tariffs and other barriers on trade among its members, which makes it cheaper and easier to buy and sell across borders.

ww.Sets the prices of all goods sold among: Prices are still set by markets and not by the agreement, which does not fix the prices of goods traded among the member countries.
ww.Raises tariffs on all goods that members: Raising tariffs on all goods among members would reduce trade and defeat the purpose of the agreement, which is to cut such taxes.
ww.Bans exports of goods between the member: Banning exports between members would end trade among them, and this is the opposite of a free trade agreement, which opens markets to more trade.

rw: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up when making a choice, such as the best other use of your time or money.

ww.The profit a business earns after paying: The profit left after paying expenses is net income, which is a measure of a firm's earnings and not the value of a forgone alternative.
ww.The extra fee charged when ordering at a: An extra fee for ordering is a service charge, which is a money cost, whereas opportunity cost concerns the best alternative you give up.
ww.The total dollar price paid when buying: The dollar price paid is the monetary cost, which ignores the value of the alternative given up, and that forgone alternative is what opportunity cost measures.

rw: Scarcity arises because resources are limited while human wants are unlimited, so people cannot have everything and must choose among alternatives, giving up some options.

ww.Money has no value in modern economies t: Money has value in modern economies and is widely used, so claiming it has none is false, and scarcity comes from limited resources, not from worthless money.
ww.Businesses refuse to produce enough good: Scarcity exists because resources are limited, not because businesses refuse to produce, and even willing producers cannot satisfy every want with finite inputs.
ww.Governments ban most products so no one: Governments do not ban most products, and scarcity would still exist without such bans because resources are limited relative to the wants of consumers.

rw: Labor, the work done by people, is one of the four factors of production, alongside land, capital and entrepreneurship, because it is an input used to make goods.

ww.Demand, which is the desire to buy goods: Demand is the desire and ability to buy goods, which describes consumers in a market and is not an input used in production.
ww.Profit, which is money left after all co: Profit is the money remaining after costs, a reward or result of production, and it is not one of the resources used in making goods.
ww.Inflation, which is a general rise in pr: Inflation is a general rise in prices, which is an economic condition and not a resource that businesses combine to produce goods and services.

rw: Capital in the factors of production means human made tools, machinery and buildings that are used to produce other goods and services.

ww.The money a person keeps in a savings ac: Money in a savings account is financial capital, but in economics the factor called capital means physical goods used in production rather than cash held by a person.
ww.The natural resources found beneath the: Natural resources found in the ground belong to the factor called land, which includes everything provided by nature, and not capital.
ww.The skills that an entrepreneur must hav: Skills of an entrepreneur are part of entrepreneurship or human capital, a separate idea from capital in economics, which means physical goods.

rw: An entrepreneur brings together land, labor and capital to start a business and accepts the risk of loss in the hope of profit.

ww.A person who works for a fixed wage and: A person who works for a fixed wage and has no say is an employee, not an entrepreneur, who makes decisions and bears the risk.
ww.A person who lends money to businesses a: A person who lends money to businesses and banks is a lender or investor, not an entrepreneur, who organizes and runs the venture.
ww.A person who collects taxes for the gove: Collecting taxes is the role of a government official or tax agency and has nothing to do with an entrepreneur, who starts and runs a business.

rw: Studying for the evening means giving up the wages from a shift, so one choice is gained at the expense of another, which is exactly a trade off.

ww.Buying a gift with money found on the si: Buying a gift with money found on the sidewalk involves no real sacrifice, since the money came free, so it does not clearly show giving up one thing for another.
ww.Inheriting a house from a relative in an: Inheriting a house is receiving a windfall, not choosing between alternatives, so no option is given up, which means it does not illustrate a trade off.
ww.Receiving a prize for winning a contest: Receiving a prize for winning a contest is a reward with no choice among alternatives, so it does not require giving up anything and is not a trade off.

rw: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up, which here is the $80 that the student could have earned working on Saturday.

ww.The $0 admission price to attend the fre: The workshop is free, so the admission price is $0, but opportunity cost is about the forgone earnings, not the price of attending.
ww.The cost of the workshop's materials and: Materials and books are out of pocket costs and are not the best alternative forgone, and the problem states the workshop is free, so the opportunity cost is the $80.
ww.The $160 that two Saturdays would have e: The $160 figure doubles the amount for two Saturdays, but the student gives up only one Saturday of work, so the forgone earnings are $80.

rw: The law of demand says that when the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls, and when the price falls, the quantity demanded rises.

ww.As income rises, prices must always rise: Income rising and prices rising is not what the law of demand says, which concerns the relationship between a good's own price and the quantity people buy.
ww.As price rises, quantity demanded rises: Saying quantity demanded rises as price rises reverses the law, since higher prices lead buyers to purchase less, not more, other things equal.
ww.As supply rises, demand must also rise: Supply rising does not force demand to rise, and the law of demand links price and quantity demanded, not the supply and demand curves themselves.

rw: The law of supply states that as the price of a good rises, producers are willing to supply a larger quantity, because higher prices mean more profit.

ww.As price rises, quantity supplied falls: Quantity supplied falling as price rises would reverse the law of supply, since higher prices give producers an incentive to sell more.
ww.As costs rise, producers always make mor: Rising costs usually discourage production or push firms to produce less, so saying producers always make more as costs rise does not match the law of supply.
ww.As demand falls, prices always rise: The statement mixes demand with prices, and the law of supply links a good's own price to quantity supplied, not demand falling to higher prices.

rw: Equilibrium is the price at which the amount buyers want to purchase equals the amount sellers want to sell, so the market clears with neither surplus nor shortage.

ww.Producers earn zero revenue from their s: At equilibrium producers do sell goods and earn revenue at the market price, so claiming they earn zero revenue is not what equilibrium means.
ww.Consumers stop buying altogether in the: At equilibrium consumers keep buying at the market price, and the quantity they want equals the quantity supplied, so they do not stop buying altogether.
ww.The government has set a fixed price for: Equilibrium arises from the interaction of buyers and sellers in a free market, not from a government fixed price, which would be a price control.

rw: A price above equilibrium reduces the quantity people want while encouraging more production, so quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, which creates a surplus of unsold goods.

ww.No change, because prices never affect m: Prices affect markets strongly, since they guide how much buyers want and sellers offer, so saying prices never affect markets is not accurate.
ww.A shortage, because buyers want more tha: A shortage occurs when the price is below equilibrium and buyers want more than is available, so a price above equilibrium cannot cause it.
ww.A permanent monopoly for one seller of t: One seller holding a permanent monopoly is not caused by a price above equilibrium, which simply produces a surplus until the price adjusts back down.

rw: When the price is below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, so buyers cannot all get the product, which creates a shortage.

ww.A decrease in the number of buyers: A price below equilibrium makes the good cheaper, which attracts more buyers, not fewer, so the number of buyers does not decrease.
ww.A surplus, because sellers have goods: A surplus occurs when the price is above equilibrium and sellers have more than buyers want, so it does not result from a price below equilibrium.
ww.A tax refund for all of the buyers: A tax refund has nothing to do with market prices, since a price below equilibrium changes the balance of supply and demand and not taxes.

rw: Rising popularity of electric cars reduces the desire for gasoline at every price, so the demand curve for gasoline shifts to the left.

ww.A fall in the cost of crude oil and of g: A fall in the cost of crude oil lowers production costs and shifts the supply curve, not demand, so it does not move the demand curve left.
ww.A new refinery opening near a large city: A new refinery increases the supply of gasoline and so shifts the supply curve, not the demand curve, so demand does not move left.
ww.A cold winter that raises heating needs: A cold winter raising heating needs would raise demand for heating fuels, shifting demand to the right if anything, and it does not reduce gasoline demand.

rw: Wheat flour is a key input, so a higher price raises the cost of making bread, which reduces supply and shifts the supply curve to the left.

ww.A rise in consumer income levels: Higher consumer income raises demand for bread, which shifts the demand curve and not the supply curve, so it does not move supply to the left.
ww.A new fad diet that favors bread: A fad diet favoring bread raises consumer demand, shifting the demand curve to the right, and it does not shift the supply curve left.
ww.A drop in the price of bakery ovens: Cheaper ovens lower production costs for bakers, which increases supply and shifts the supply curve to the right, not to the left.

rw: A substitute good can replace another, so when one good's price rises, buyers switch to the other, which is the definition of a substitute.

ww.A product used together with another and: A product used together with another and bought alongside it is a complement, not a substitute, because complements are consumed jointly rather than in place of each other.
ww.A product that is only sold by one compa: A product sold by only one company describes a monopoly situation and says nothing about whether another good can replace it, so it is not a substitute.
ww.A product that has no price at all attac: Goods in stores have prices, so a product with no price attached is not a defined category and certainly not what a substitute good means.

rw: Complementary goods are used together, so demand for one rises and falls with the other, as with cars and gasoline or hot dogs and buns.

ww.A product that can replace another in a: A product that can replace another is a substitute, not a complement, since complements are used together, as with printers and ink, not in place of each other.
ww.A product that is sold only abroad and n: Where a product is sold does not define a complementary good, which is defined by being used together with another product, not by domestic or foreign sales.
ww.A product that is given away for free to: A product given away for free is not what complementary means, since complements are paired goods that people use together, whatever their prices may be.

rw: As hot dogs get costlier, people buy fewer of them and so need fewer buns, which means the demand for buns falls because the two are complements.

ww.Demand for buns rises, because the goods: Hot dogs and buns are used together, so they are complements, not substitutes, and a price rise for hot dogs will lower, not raise, demand for buns.
ww.Supply of buns rises immediately after t: A change in the price of hot dogs shifts the demand for buns and not supply, so saying supply of buns rises misreads the situation.
ww.Demand for buns is unchanged, because th: Hot dogs and buns are closely related goods consumed together, so the demand for buns is affected by the hot dog price and is not unchanged.

rw: Elasticity of demand measures how strongly the quantity demanded responds to a change in price, so a very responsive good has elastic demand and an unresponsive one is inelastic.

ww.How much a product costs to make in the: The cost of making a product is a production cost, whereas elasticity of demand concerns how buyers react to price changes, not what factories spend.
ww.How quickly a business can hire new work: How quickly a business can hire workers relates to labor market conditions and has nothing to do with how buyers respond to a price change.
ww.How long a product lasts before it break: How long a product lasts is its durability, an unrelated product trait, whereas elasticity of demand describes how the quantity bought responds to price.

rw: Insulin is a medical necessity with no close substitute, so a patient keeps buying it even if the price rises, which makes demand inelastic.

ww.A particular brand of potato chips: Many other chip brands exist, so shoppers can switch if one brand gets pricier, making demand for a particular brand elastic and not inelastic.
ww.A luxury vacation package abroad: A luxury vacation is not essential and can be postponed or replaced, so buyers cut back when prices rise, which makes demand elastic.
ww.A restaurant meal on a weeknight: A restaurant meal on a weeknight can be replaced by cooking at home, so diners respond readily to price changes, which means demand is elastic.

rw: When demand is elastic, the percentage drop in quantity demanded exceeds the percentage rise in price, so total revenue, price times quantity, falls.

ww.Total revenue stays exactly the same aft: With elastic demand, a price rise changes quantity sold by a large amount, so revenue cannot stay exactly the same after the price increase.
ww.Total revenue doubles automatically when: Revenue does not automatically double, because a higher price also reduces quantity sold, and with elastic demand the lost sales outweigh the extra revenue per unit.
ww.Total revenue rises, as the price increa: This describes inelastic demand, where the price gain outweighs the loss in sales; with elastic demand the quantity drop is larger, so revenue falls instead.

rw: Marginal utility is the additional satisfaction a consumer gets from consuming one more unit of a good, and it usually declines as more is consumed.

ww.Fixed overhead: Fixed overhead is a cost that does not change with output, so it describes a business expense and not the extra satisfaction a consumer gets from another unit.
ww.Opportunity cost: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative given up, not the added satisfaction from consuming one more unit of a good.
ww.Total revenue: Total revenue is price times quantity sold, a business measure, and it does not describe a consumer's added satisfaction from consuming a further unit.

rw: The law of diminishing marginal utility states that each additional unit consumed gives less added satisfaction than the one before it, as when a third slice of pizza satisfies less.

ww.Prices always fall as consumption rises,: Prices do not automatically fall with consumption, and the law concerns satisfaction, not price, so this statement does not describe diminishing marginal utility.
ww.Each additional unit consumed gives more: More added satisfaction from each further unit would be increasing marginal utility, the opposite of the law, which says added satisfaction declines as consumption grows.
ww.Total satisfaction always falls with eac: Total satisfaction usually keeps rising, only more slowly, while the added satisfaction falls, so saying total satisfaction always falls misreads the law of diminishing marginal utility.

rw: A loaf of bread bought by a family for dinner is sold to its final user, so it counts as a final good in GDP.

ww.Sugar bought by a factory to make cookie: Sugar bought by a factory is used to make cookies, so it is an intermediate good, and counting it would double count its value in GDP.
ww.Yeast bought by a bakery to make the dou: Yeast bought by a bakery for dough is an input in further production, which makes it an intermediate good that GDP excludes to avoid double counting.
ww.Flour bought by a bakery to make bread f: Flour bought by a bakery to make bread is an intermediate good, because its value is included later in the price of the finished bread, so GDP leaves it out.

rw: Their value is already included in the price of the final good, so adding them separately would count the same value more than once.

ww.They have no economic value in the marke: Intermediate goods do have economic value and are sold in markets, so saying they have none is false, and the reason for excluding them is double counting.
ww.Intermediate goods are always illegal to: Intermediate goods are legal products that firms buy and sell every day, so claiming they are illegal to sell is false and is not why GDP excludes them.
ww.They are produced abroad and never count: Intermediate goods are often produced at home, and where they are made is not the reason for exclusion; the reason is avoiding double counting.

rw: The expenditure approach adds consumption, investment, government spending and net exports, giving GDP as the total of spending on final goods and services, often written C plus I plus G plus NX.

ww.Wages, rent, interest and profit paid to: Wages, rent, interest and profit are income categories used in the income approach to GDP, not the four spending components of the expenditure approach.
ww.Supply, demand, price and quantity in a: Supply, demand, price and quantity are market concepts used to analyze individual markets, and they are not the components of GDP in the expenditure approach.
ww.Land, labor, capital and enterprise in a: Land, labor, capital and enterprise are the factors of production, which are inputs to output, and not the spending categories that make up GDP.

rw: GDP equals 700 plus 150 plus 200 plus net exports of 90 minus 110, which is negative 20, so 1,050 minus 20 gives $1,030.

ww.$1,090: The figure $1,090 does not follow the formula; GDP is C plus I plus G plus net exports, and net exports of 90 minus 110 equal negative 20.
ww.$1,250: The figure $1,250 comes from adding both exports and imports to the other components, but imports must be subtracted, so net exports are negative 20 and GDP is $1,030.
ww.$1,050: The figure $1,050 sums only consumption, investment and government spending, 700 plus 150 plus 200, and leaves out net exports of negative 20, so the correct GDP is $1,030.

rw: Real GDP is adjusted for inflation, so it shows output at constant prices, while nominal GDP uses current prices and can rise just because prices went up.

ww.Nominal GDP leaves out state spending; r: Both nominal and real GDP include government spending, so the difference between them is about adjusting for price changes, not about leaving out state spending.
ww.There is no difference between the two k: There is a difference, since nominal GDP uses current prices while real GDP is adjusted for inflation, so the two can move differently when prices change.
ww.Real GDP counts only exports; nominal GD: Both measures count all components, including exports and imports, so real GDP does not count only exports; the distinction is the inflation adjustment.

rw: A recession is a significant decline in economic activity spread across the economy that lasts several months, shown in falling output, jobs and incomes.

ww.A short rise in stock prices over one we: A short rise in stock prices over one week is a market gain, not a recession, which is a significant decline in the economy lasting several months.
ww.A time when the government collects extr: A government collecting extra taxes is a fiscal matter and does not define a recession, which is marked by falling output, income and employment.
ww.A period in which prices fall for one pr: A price fall for one product is a relative price change in a single market, whereas a recession is a broad decline in economic activity.

rw: The business cycle is the repeating pattern of expansion and contraction in economic activity, moving through peaks, recessions, troughs and recoveries over the years.

ww.The path of money from a bank to a borro: The path of money from a bank to a borrower describes lending, and it has nothing to do with the economy's pattern of expansion and decline.
ww.The steps a firm follows to make one pro: The steps a firm follows to make one product describe a production process inside one company, not the economy wide fluctuations known as the business cycle.
ww.The yearly calendar of a company's sales: A company's yearly sales calendar is a marketing schedule and not the economy wide pattern of rising and falling activity that defines the business cycle.

rw: During expansion the economy grows, so output, employment and income all rise, which is the typical sign of the expansion phase of the business cycle.

ww.The economy stops producing most goods: An economy in expansion keeps producing goods and in fact produces more, so saying it stops producing most goods describes a severe collapse, not expansion.
ww.Output, employment and income all fall: Output, employment and income all falling describes a contraction or recession, which is the opposite of what happens during an expansion.
ww.Prices become fixed by law for goods: Prices are not fixed by law during an expansion, because markets still set prices, so this has no link to the expansion phase.

rw: The trough is the lowest point of the business cycle, where output bottoms out after a contraction before the recovery begins.

ww.The peak: The peak is the highest point of the cycle, where expansion ends and contraction begins, so it is the top, not the lowest point.
ww.The recovery: Recovery is the phase after the lowest point, when output starts to rise again, so it follows the bottom rather than being the lowest point.
ww.The expansion: Expansion is the phase in which output grows, so it is a rising period and not the lowest point of the cycle.

rw: Productivity is the amount of output produced per unit of input, such as goods made per hour of labor, so higher productivity means more output from the same resources.

ww.The total number of workers hired: The total number of workers hired is a measure of employment, not productivity, which compares how much output is produced with the inputs used.
ww.The price at which goods are sold: The price at which goods are sold is a market price and is not productivity, which measures output in relation to the inputs used.
ww.The wages paid to each worker: Wages paid to each worker are labor income, and they do not measure how much output each unit of input generates, which is productivity.

rw: Better equipment and training let each worker produce more in the same time, so output per hour rises and labor productivity increases directly.

ww.Making workers stay longer with no extra: Longer hours with no extra tools may add some output but not per hour, and tired workers may even produce less, so productivity is not directly raised.
ww.Reducing the number of machines in the f: Reducing the number of machines gives each worker less capital to use, which lowers output per worker, so it would reduce labor productivity.
ww.Cutting worker training budgets and pay: Cutting training budgets and pay weakens skills and morale, which tends to lower output per worker, so it would not raise labor productivity.

rw: Specialization means focusing on a limited range of goods or tasks, so people and firms become more efficient at them, which raises output and gains from trade.

ww.Hiring workers who have no skills for th: Hiring workers who have no skills for the job would lower efficiency and does not describe specialization, which means concentrating on what one does best.
ww.Making every product in one workshop so: Making every product in a single workshop is the opposite of specialization, because it spreads effort across many products instead of concentrating on a few.
ww.Buying goods only from foreign suppliers: Buying goods only from foreign suppliers is an import choice and not specialization, which concerns narrowing what one produces and not where goods are purchased.

rw: Division of labor splits production into separate tasks assigned to different workers, so each becomes skilled at one step and total output rises.

ww.Dividing the profits among all sharehold: Dividing profits among shareholders is a dividend distribution and not division of labor, which concerns splitting up the tasks of production among workers.
ww.Giving all workers identical jobs in a s: Giving all workers identical jobs is the opposite of division of labor, which assigns different tasks to different workers.
ww.Splitting a large company into two firms: Splitting a large company into two firms is a corporate restructuring and does not describe division of labor, which divides work tasks among workers inside production.

rw: As a medium of exchange, money is accepted for goods and services, which avoids the need for a double coincidence of wants required in bartering, so trade is easier.

ww.To make goods hard to trade at all: Money makes trade easier, not harder, so claiming its purpose is to make goods hard to trade reverses its role as a medium of exchange.
ww.To replace all work with leisure: Money does not replace work with leisure, and people still work to earn it, so this misstates the purpose of money as a medium of exchange.
ww.To ensure prices never change at all: Money cannot guarantee that prices never change, since prices move with supply and demand, and this is not what a medium of exchange does.

rw: Store of value is the function that lets people keep purchasing power, saving money today so it can be spent later on goods and services.

ww.Medium of exchange: A medium of exchange is what people use to buy and sell goods, which is a different function from holding purchasing power to use later.
ww.Deferred payment: Deferred payment lets people buy now and pay later, as with loans and credit, which is different from saving purchasing power for future use.
ww.Unit of account: A unit of account is a common measure for stating prices and values, which is a different job from keeping purchasing power over time.

rw: Prices rose by 5% while pay rose only 2%, so the worker can afford less than before, and real purchasing power falls by roughly 3%.

ww.It doubles, because both figures are pos: Purchasing power does not double just because both numbers are positive, and prices rising faster than pay means the worker can buy less.
ww.It rises, because pay increased in the y: Pay rose by 2%, but prices rose 5%, a larger amount, so the worker's money buys less and purchasing power falls despite the raise.
ww.It stays the same, as both prices and wa: Both rose, but not by the same amount; the 5% price rise exceeds the 2% pay rise, so purchasing power does not stay the same.

rw: Deflation is a general, sustained decline in the level of prices over time, so each unit of money buys more goods and services than before.

ww.A fall in the supply of money to almost: A fall in the money supply to nearly zero is a monetary contraction and not the definition of deflation, which concerns falling prices in general.
ww.A general rise in the level of prices ov: A general rise in the price level is inflation, not deflation, which is the reverse and refers to prices falling over time.
ww.A rise in the number of unemployed worke: A rise in unemployed workers is a labor market change, not a definition of deflation, which describes a general decline in prices.

rw: Unemployment describes people who are able and willing to work and are looking for jobs but cannot find them, so they count as part of the labor force.

ww.The condition of people who choose to st: People who choose to stay home and not look for work are not counted as unemployed, since unemployment requires actively seeking a job.
ww.The condition of people who work part-ti: People who work part-time by choice and are happy with the hours are employed and content, so they are not unemployed under the standard definition.
ww.The condition of people who are retired: Retired people who no longer wish to work are outside the labor force, so they are not counted as unemployed.

rw: Structural unemployment arises when workers' skills no longer match available jobs because of technology or industry change, so these workers must move to other industries.

ww.Frictional unemployment: Frictional unemployment is the short time spent between jobs or while searching, and it does not describe workers displaced when an industry shrinks because of new technology.
ww.Cyclical unemployment: Cyclical unemployment comes from downturns in the business cycle, but this factory closed because consumers moved to a new technology, not because of a recession.
ww.Seasonal unemployment: Seasonal unemployment follows regular yearly patterns such as holiday or summer work, but this closure came from a lasting technology shift and not from the calendar.

rw: Seasonal unemployment occurs when work depends on the time of year, and ski instruction is available only in winter, so the instructor is jobless each summer.

ww.Structural unemployment: Structural unemployment comes from lasting industry or technology changes, but a ski instructor's work disappears every summer on a predictable seasonal basis, not permanently.
ww.Cyclical unemployment: Cyclical unemployment follows the downs of the business cycle, but this instructor loses work every summer regardless of how the overall economy is doing.
ww.Frictional unemployment: Frictional unemployment is the short search time between jobs, but the instructor is out of work for the whole summer because skiing is seasonal.

rw: An economic system is the way a society decides what to produce, how to produce it and for whom, so it answers the basic questions of scarcity.

ww.The set of machines used in a large fact: The set of machines in a factory is part of its capital and not an economic system, which is how a whole society organizes its production.
ww.The rules of a single company's board of: The rules of one company's board govern a single firm, while an economic system is the way an entire society organizes production and distribution.
ww.The list of taxes that a country charges: A list of taxes is only one part of government policy and not an economic system, which decides what and for whom to produce.

rw: Every economic system must decide what to produce, how to produce it and for whom, because resources are scarce and wants are not.

ww.When to tax, whom to fine and where to b: Deciding when to tax, whom to fine and where to build are government choices, not the three basic questions that every economic system must answer.
ww.Which bank to use, how to save and when: Which bank to use, how to save and when to retire are personal finance choices and not the basic questions that all economic systems answer.
ww.Who to hire, where to advertise and what: Who to hire, where to advertise and what to charge are business decisions within one firm and are not the three basic questions every economic system answers.

rw: In a market economy, consumers and producers acting through prices decide what is made, because their buying and selling choices signal what is wanted and profitable.

ww.A foreign trade agency in another countr: A foreign trade agency in another country does not direct what a domestic market economy produces, since decisions come from local consumers and producers.
ww.A central government office that sets al: A central government office setting all outputs describes a command economy, not a market economy, where decisions are spread among buyers and sellers.
ww.A royal family or tribal leader in each: A royal family or tribal leader deciding for a region describes a traditional economy ruled by custom, and not a market economy driven by prices.

rw: In a command economy, the central government decides what to produce, how much and for whom, so it makes most economic decisions.

ww.Local families by custom: Local families following custom describes a traditional economy, whereas in a command economy the central authority, not families or custom, makes most decisions.
ww.Individual consumers: Individual consumers guiding production through their purchases is a feature of a market economy and not a command economy, where planners decide.
ww.Competing private firms: Competing private firms making decisions is a mark of a market economy, while in a command economy the state controls most production.

rw: In a traditional economy, customs and habits handed down over generations guide what is produced and traded, so decisions follow established practice.

ww.An economy in which only exports are all: Allowing only exports is a trade restriction and not a type of economy, so it does not describe a traditional economy based on custom.
ww.An economy in which computers make all o: Computers making all the decisions for firms is not a recognized economic system and does not describe a traditional economy, which relies on custom and habit.
ww.An economy in which a central office set: A central office setting every price and all output describes a command economy, which is the opposite of a traditional economy guided by custom.

rw: A mixed economy combines private economic choice with some government involvement, such as regulation and public services, and the United States is a common example.

ww.An economy based only on bartering goods: An economy based only on bartering is a barter system, and it does not describe a mixed economy, which blends private choice with government involvement.
ww.An economy with no government role at al: An economy with no government role at all would be a pure market economy, which is the opposite of a mixed economy.
ww.An economy with no private firms at all: An economy with no private firms would be a pure command economy, which differs from a mixed economy that includes both private and public roles.

rw: The United States is mostly market based but the government also regulates and provides services, so it is a mixed economy that leans toward the market.

ww.A pure command economy run by the state: The United States is not a pure command economy, because private firms and consumers make most decisions, and the state does not run the economy.
ww.A traditional economy based on custom: The modern United States relies on markets, technology and laws more than custom, so describing it as a traditional economy is wrong.
ww.A barter economy with no money at all: The United States uses money and markets widely, so calling it a barter economy with no money at all is plainly wrong.

rw: Capitalism is a system in which private owners control the means of production, such as factories and land, and operate them to earn profit.

ww.A system in which people trade only by c: Trading only by custom describes a traditional economy, whereas capitalism is based on private ownership and markets, with profit as a motive.
ww.A system in which prices are set by law: Prices set only by law would describe a controlled or command system, while in capitalism prices are mostly set by supply and demand.
ww.A system in which the government owns al: Government ownership of all property describes communism or a pure command system, which is the opposite of capitalism, where private owners hold property.

rw: In socialism the state or community owns major industries and resources and directs them for shared benefit, instead of leaving them to private owners.

ww.A system in which no taxes are collected: Socialism does not mean that no taxes are collected, and in fact such systems usually rely on taxes to fund public ownership and services.
ww.A system in which individuals own all bu: Individuals owning all businesses describes capitalism or private enterprise, which is the opposite of socialism, where major industries are collectively owned.
ww.A system in which trade is banned by law: Socialism does not ban trade, because socialist countries still trade, and the defining feature is public or collective ownership of major industries.

rw: Profit rewards entrepreneurs for taking risk and signals where resources are wanted, since high profits attract producers to the goods that consumers value.

ww.It guarantees that every business will s: Profit does not guarantee success, because many firms lose money and fail, so it is a reward and signal and not a promise.
ww.It is set by the government for each fir: In a market economy profit is earned by firms in the market, not set by the government for each business, so this statement is false.
ww.It is banned by law for all firms in eve: Profit is not banned in a market economy, because it is the main motive and reward for businesses, so this option is false.

rw: Private property means individuals and firms have the right to own, use and sell resources, which gives them an incentive to use those resources productively.

ww.The duty to share all goods equally with: Sharing all goods equally describes communal ownership, whereas private property is the right of individuals and firms to own and use resources for themselves.
ww.The rule that no one may sell what they: Private property includes the right to sell what you own, so a rule that no one may sell their property contradicts the idea.
ww.The right of the government to seize any: Private property rights protect owners from arbitrary seizure, so the government's right to take assets without paying is the opposite of the idea.

rw: Competition among sellers for customers is typical of a market economy, as firms try to offer better prices and quality to win buyers.

ww.Jobs assigned by birth and tradition: Jobs assigned by birth and tradition are typical of a traditional economy and not a market economy, where people choose their work.
ww.A single planner setting every price: A single planner setting every price describes a command economy, whereas in a market economy prices come from the interaction of buyers and sellers.
ww.A ban on private businesses of any kind: A market economy allows and relies on private businesses, so a ban on them describes a command economy and is not a feature of a market.

rw: Consumer sovereignty means consumers' buying choices determine what producers make, since firms must supply what people want to buy in order to earn profit.

ww.Producers decide what consumers may buy: If producers decided what consumers may buy, consumers would lack power, which is the opposite of consumer sovereignty, where buyers direct production.
ww.The government decides what consumers mu: Government deciding what consumers must buy describes central control, not consumer sovereignty, in which consumers' own choices guide the market.
ww.Consumers must buy only domestic goods m: Consumer sovereignty lets consumers buy domestic or foreign goods, so a requirement to buy only domestic goods contradicts the idea of consumer choice.

rw: Smith's invisible hand says that when people pursue their own self interest in markets, society can benefit, as if guided by an unseen force to good outcomes.

ww.A secret government agency sets all pric: The invisible hand is a metaphor for market forces and not a secret agency, and Smith argued against central control of prices.
ww.A rule that businesses must give away pr: The invisible hand does not require giving away profits, because it relies on people pursuing their own gain, and it is not a rule about profits.
ww.A hidden tax that businesses pay each ye: The invisible hand is not a hidden tax; it is a metaphor for how self interested choices in markets can serve the wider society.

rw: In a free enterprise system, private businesses operate with limited government control, free to choose what to make, how to make it and what to charge.

ww.A system in which no one may earn a prof: Free enterprise permits profit, since the possibility of earning profit is a key motive, so a system banning all profit is not free enterprise.
ww.A system in which the state runs all fir: A system where the state runs all firms and shops is a command economy, the opposite of free enterprise, where private businesses operate freely.
ww.A system in which every product is free: Free enterprise refers to freedom to run a business, not to products being given away, so a system where every product is free is not what it means.

rw: A central agency deciding how many cars each factory must build shows the government planning production, which is the hallmark of a command economy.

ww.A bakery lowers prices to attract custom: A bakery cutting prices to compete is a market decision made by a private firm, which is not an example of central planning in a command economy.
ww.A student chooses between two job offers: A student choosing between two job offers is an individual choice made freely, which reflects market freedom and not central direction in a command economy.
ww.A family farm follows ancestral methods: A family farm following ancestral methods shows a traditional economy guided by custom, not a command economy where a central authority makes the decisions.

rw: Without market prices, planners cannot easily tell what people want or what goods cost to make, so the command economy risks shortages and surpluses, a known weakness.

ww.Too many firms compete for customers: Many firms competing for customers is a feature of market economies, and it is not a weakness of command economies where the state controls production.
ww.Prices rise and fall too quickly to foll: Prices in a command economy are set by planners and do not move quickly, so rapid price changes are not its weakness.
ww.Consumers choose too many varieties to b: Consumers choosing among many varieties is a feature of market economies, whereas command economies often have limited choices, so this is not their weakness.

rw: Because private firms seek profit, pure markets may underprovide public goods and leave some people without access, which is a recognized weakness of market economies.

ww.The government owns all property in the: Government ownership of all property describes a command economy, so it cannot be a weakness of a pure market economy, where property is privately held.
ww.A central plan decides everything for ev: A central plan deciding everything for every consumer describes a command economy and not a pure market economy, which relies on individual choices.
ww.Customs prevent change in the way goods: Customs preventing change is a feature of traditional economies, while market economies change quickly with competition, so this is not their weakness.

rw: A public good is open to everyone, and one person's use leaves enough for others, like a lighthouse or national defense, so it is nonrival and nonexcludable.

ww.A good that is used up by a single perso: A good used up by a single person at a time is a private good, whereas a public good is available to all and is not used up.
ww.A good that only wealthy people can buy: A good only wealthy people can buy is a private or luxury good, and a public good is available to everyone regardless of wealth.
ww.A good that is sold at a store for a pro: A good sold in stores for profit is a private good, and public goods are usually provided by government because sellers cannot easily charge users.

rw: An externality is a cost or benefit that reaches people who were not involved in the transaction, such as pollution from a factory affecting neighbors.

ww.A tax collected on imported goods at the: A tax collected on imported goods is a tariff, not an externality, which is a side effect of an activity on uninvolved third parties.
ww.A fee charged by a bank for services it: A fee charged by a bank is a direct cost paid by the customer in the transaction, and not an externality, which affects uninvolved parties.
ww.A profit earned by a business owner each: A profit earned by a business owner is a gain for a party in the transaction, not an externality, which falls on people uninvolved in it.

rw: The factory's pollution imposes cleanup costs on residents who are not part of its business, which is a cost reaching uninvolved people and so a negative externality.

ww.A public good only: Pollution harms residents rather than giving shared benefits, so it is not a public good, which is open to all and benefits everyone.
ww.A positive externality: A positive externality gives uninvolved people a benefit, but here residents bear cleanup costs, so the spillover is harmful and is a negative externality.
ww.Economic equilibrium: Equilibrium is where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded and it does not describe a cost imposed on uninvolved residents by a polluting factory.

rw: The homeowner's action gives neighbors a benefit they did not pay for, which is a benefit reaching uninvolved people, so it is a positive externality.

ww.A monopoly position: A monopoly means one seller controls a market, and a homeowner's garden is not a business, so it does not describe this situation.
ww.A trade deficit gap: A trade deficit means imports exceed exports between countries, and a homeowner planting a garden has nothing to do with international trade.
ww.A negative externality: A negative externality imposes costs on others, but neighbors enjoying the garden for free receive a benefit, so this is not negative.

rw: The free rider problem arises when people benefit from a good without paying for it, which makes it hard for private firms to fund public goods.

ww.People pay more than their fair share of: Paying more than a fair share of taxes is a fairness complaint, not the free rider problem, where people use a good without paying.
ww.People take rides at a discount on buses: Getting discounted rides on buses and trains is a price discount for riders and is not the free rider problem, where people avoid paying entirely.
ww.People refuse to use public goods at all: Free riders do use public goods, which is the problem, so saying people refuse to use them at all is the reverse of the issue.

rw: Because public goods benefit everyone and no one can be excluded, private firms cannot easily charge all who benefit, so the government provides them and funds them through taxes.

ww.Citizens refuse to use goods that are pr: Citizens do not refuse privately provided goods, and that is not why governments provide public goods, which is a problem of payment.
ww.Public goods are always unprofitable by: Public goods are not unprofitable by law, since no law says so, and the real problem is that charging users is hard.
ww.Private firms are banned from making goo: Private firms are not banned from making goods, and the government provides public goods because firms cannot easily earn payment from them.

rw: A fixed cost stays the same no matter how much is produced, as with rent or insurance, so it is the same at zero output as at high output.

ww.A cost that cannot be known in advance b: A cost that cannot be known in advance is an uncertain cost, whereas a fixed cost is a known amount that does not vary with output.
ww.A cost that is paid only when a product: A cost paid only when a product is sold describes a variable cost, like a sales commission, while a fixed cost is paid whether or not anything sells.
ww.A cost that rises with every unit produc: A cost that rises with every unit produced is a variable cost, such as materials, which is the opposite of a fixed cost that stays constant.
